name: Methotrexate for alopecia

lead: Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant prescribed off-label for alopecia areata, alone or with corticosteroids, to regrow patchy hair lost to autoimmune attack.

By suppressing immune activity it lessens the attack on follicles. A 2019 meta-analysis described definitive evidence as scarce; most data come from small studies, case series and retrospective cohorts, and newer JAK inhibitors are now compared against it in trials.

paras: It is a prescription drug taken under medical supervision with regular monitoring, and regrowth is judged over months.
It is a systemic immunosuppressant needing medical monitoring. A report described raised liver enzymes after scalp delivery sessions.

angle.text: Methotrexate suppresses immune activity, so follicles face less autoimmune attack and patchy hair can regrow in alopecia areata. It is used off-label, alone or with corticosteroids, and a 2019 meta-analysis found data mostly from small studies.

lead: Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant used in several skin diseases that has been tried off-label for alopecia areata, an autoimmune hair loss condition, either alone or alongside corticosteroids.[1][2] A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis described a paucity of definitive evidence and guidelines for this use.[1]
Evidence consists mainly of small studies, case series and retrospective cohorts.[2][3][4] Registered trials have compared it with newer agents such as tofacitinib and with other treatments.[5][6]
infobox: Oral (also injected or applied in some reports)

paras: The 2019 meta-analysis examined methotrexate as monotherapy and as an adjunct to corticosteroids, and compared combination with stand-alone use.[1] A Brazilian study evaluated efficacy and safety in alopecia areata in patients with chronic disease.[2] A French real-life evaluation looked at pulse corticosteroid plus methotrexate, and a later patient-reported study followed long-term perceptions of methylprednisolone pulses with or without methotrexate.[3][7] A report of three cases described its use in individual patients.[4] A 1973 Lancet letter on methotrexate and alopecia is an early reference in the literature.[8]

One report documented elevated transaminases after sessions in which methotrexate was delivered into the scalp by a drug-delivery technique, raising questions about systemic absorption; the report prompted published comment and a reply from the authors.[9][10][11] Methotrexate more generally is a systemic immunosuppressant requiring monitoring, according to the studies cited above.[1][2]

Registered trials include a Phase 3 study of methotrexate in severe alopecia areata (NCT02037191), a comparison with triamcinolone acetonide in recalcitrant disease, a pediatric comparison with cyclosporine, a microneedling combination, a topical methotrexate versus minoxidil trial, and a Phase 4 tofacitinib versus methotrexate trial.[5][6][12][13][14][15] Published studies are summarized above.[1][2][3]
